reply_text:
I'd admit this one: **pass**. The quote is word for word on Google's own page, and it meets all four parts of the rule.

**The page.** The link opened. It is Google's blog post "Q3 2026 earnings call: Remarks from our CEO". The byline is Sundar Pichai and the page is dated 2026-10-28. The quote appears exactly as given, in the Gemini/models section:

> "This rapid progress underscores our incredible model momentum. We're at the point where AI is helping us increase our training and launch velocity. I would expect the next 12 months to see continued acceleration because of RSI."

This is the company printing the speaker's own prepared remarks, not a news report. It counts as a primary source.

**The four parts of the rule:**
1. **Role: met.** On 2026-10-28 Pichai was chief executive of Google (since 2015) and of Alphabet (since 2019). Google builds the Gemini models and its own AI chips (TPUs).
2. **Looks forward and is about AI: met.** He predicts that AI progress will keep speeding up because AI is helping to train and launch models (recursive self-improvement, "RSI"). That is about what AI will do, not about spending or capacity, and it isn't framed as a hypothetical. One point for the reviewer: "acceleration" is vague, and the sentence before it is about Google's training and launch speed. I don't read it as a business forecast or as truly borderline. A similarly vague forecast already admitted, 2024-12-04 "progress harder in 2025", supports that reading.
3. **Date or length of time: met.** "The next 12 months" is a stated length of time counted from the day it was said, so it runs to about 2027-10-28.
4. **Primary source: met.** As above, these are his own remarks on Google's site.

**Not already recorded.** None of his recorded claim files makes this claim. The closest, 2024-12-04 "progress harder in 2025", is a different forecast with a different date.

**Likely status: `unfalsifiable`.** "Continued acceleration" names no condition an outsider could check, so the bar should probably be set that way when the claim is entered. That affects how the claim is scored, not whether it gets in.
